p.title: LobbyView: Firm-level Lobbying & Congressional Bills Database

ext.title: LobbyView: Firm-level Lobbying & Congressional Bills Database
ext.venue: Working paper, MIT Department of Political Science (draft dated August 30, 2018). No journal or series named in the text.
ext.document_type: Working paper / technical database documentation (partial; the text says the full methods description will come later)
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 378 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\68dd7ab2a4fc.txt (front matter, Abstract, Sections 1 through 5.5, including references). The text is a technical manual, so there are no statistical results, regressions or network estimates to read. Metadata hint corrected: the title, author, date and "working paper (MIT)" label match the text; no DOI is given. No Paul markup file was supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: No explicit research question. The document describes and documents the LobbyView database, which links congressional bill sponsorship with lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995, and the API used to bulk-download it (Abstract; Section 1).
ext.theory: No theory section. The Abstract gives the motivation only: lobbying by special interest groups matters for policymaking, and empirical studies of political representation have been limited by the difficulty of observing a direct link between politicians and interest groups.
ext.data: Source: the universe of lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 (Abstract). Units named in the text: lobbying reports, lobbying issue sections ("specific issues"), bills (ids of the form "110_HR7311", Section 5.2), firms/clients, and industries (NAICS2 groupings, Section 5.5). Sample size N: not reported. Time period: not stated as a single range; the CONGRESSES setting in general.py sets the range and its default values are not given (Section 4.1). Example years used in the text are illustrative (2002 Mattel report, 2011 filter example, 2013 Google report). Firm financials come from Compustat (Section 5.5.2), and industry codes from NAICS and SIC. The 52,418 count in Section 5.3 is a query result over all loaded reports that carry the TRADE (DOMESTIC/FOREIGN) issue; the text gives no year restriction for it.
ext.method: Descriptive data construction, not statistical estimation. Bills in reports are found by regular-expression search for bill numbers (Section 2, step 1). The Congress is assigned by maximizing the cosine similarity between a bag-of-words vector of each candidate bill and a vector of the text around the bill mention, over the candidate Congresses (Section 2, step 2, Eq. 1). Congress numbers propagate across a report, with majority vote where bills disagree (step 3). Bill titles are matched to report text (step 4). Bill ranges are expanded (step 5). Storage uses SQLite with SQLAlchemy and Elixir, and full-text search uses Whoosh over CRS summaries and specific issues (Sections 3.1, 5.4). Herfindahl indices are computed per industry (herfindahl.py), then augmented with a trade-issue indicator and Compustat data (herfindadd.py) (Section 5.5).
ext.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim and presents no identification strategy.
ext.scope: Population: lobbying reports and firms/clients under the LDA (1995 onward). Institution: US Congress bills and their sponsorship. Era: post-1995 LDA filings, with the Congress range set in configuration. Stated purpose: enable systematic research on lobbying and merging with external datasets (Abstract).

key_findings.finding: LobbyView is built from the universe of LDA lobbying reports and links bill sponsorship to reported lobbying, with firm- and industry-level identifiers and an API for bulk download.
Naive assignment of a bill to the filing-year Congress fails. The Google 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is from the 112th Congress, not the 113th.

Congress identification considers the three preceding Congresses by default and picks the candidate bill with the highest cosine similarity to the report text. If no same-numbered bill exists, the filing-year Congress is used.
Congress assignment propagates to other bills in the same report, since reports cover a single Congress. Majority vote is used if bills disagree, and the text says this rarely occurs in practice.

Bill range expansion treats close bill numbers as lobbied together. The default takes numbers with the same prefix that differ by at most 10 and expands the range. The Mattel 2002 example expands H.R.4182-4186 into five bills.
The trade-issue filter on the lobbying reports returns 52,418 reports that include the TRADE (DOMESTIC/FOREIGN) issue.
The Herfindahl index measures competition among firms (clients) within an industry. Output is per year per classification system (NAICS or SIC), and the example run covers 1996 to 2011 with NAICS.

limitations: The author says the document contains only some technical details and that the full methods description (NLP disambiguation of interest group names, collaborative filtering, PostgreSQL/Elasticsearch storage, scalability, descriptive and statistical analyses) will follow (Section 1).
Sample size, the period covered, and the default CONGRESSES range are not reported.
TEST MODE for bill detection is described as incomplete, and the text warns against enabling it (Section 4.1).
Setup from scratch may take up to several days (Section 4.2).
Setup is tied to the author's Della/tigress environment and paths (Sections 4.1, 4.2).
If no bill number matches in the Congress range, the code guesses the filing-year Congress, which can be wrong (Section 2, step 2).
Bill-title and range matching are heuristic and their error rates are not reported.

short_quotes.quote: This document currently contains only some technical details of the database.

measures: Cosine similarity between bag-of-words vectors of candidate bills and report text (Eq. 1)
Herfindahl index of firm competition within an industry (NAICS2 or SIC groupings)
Trade-issue indicator per firm (lobbied on at least one trade issue)
Counts of lobbying reports matching a filter (e.g., 52,418 with the TRADE issue)
Compustat firm-level financial data merged to firms
references_of_note: Kim, In Song. 2017. "Political Cleavages within Industry: Firm-level Lobbying for Trade Liberalization." American Political Science Review 111 (1): 1-20. (Firm-level lobbying data that the database supports.)

Kim, In Song, and Dmitriy Kunisky. 2018. "Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics." Working paper (network.pdf). (Lobbying networks in legislative politics; the closest network-analysis companion work.)
Compustat firm financial data, named in Section 5.5.2 as the source merged into herfindadd.py output.
NAICS and SIC industry classifications, used as the industry grouping (Section 5.5).

rel.summary_md:
Kim's 2018 LobbyView note is a partial technical manual, not an empirical study. It has no estimates, no N and no stated coverage window. It documents how LDA lobbying reports get linked to congressional bills. First, a regex finds bill numbers. Then each mention is assigned to a Congress by taking the argmax of cosine similarity between the candidate bill text and the text around the mention, looking back three Congresses by default; if nothing matches, the code falls back to the filing-year Congress. The Congress is then propagated across the report by majority vote, titles are matched, and close bill numbers (gap of 10 or less) are expanded into ranges. Industries are grouped by NAICS2/SIC for per-industry Herfindahl indices, with Compustat merged in. The note names one failure case: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is a 112th-Congress bill, so the naive filing-year rule gets it wrong. It gives no error rates for any heuristic.

This matters for Paul's lobbying lane in three ways:
1. **Every LobbyView-derived member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record.** That backs the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.
2. **Paul's own LDA rebuild uses a different bill-resolution rule than the LobbyView pipeline.** A citation without an "of 20XX" suffix binds to the filing-year Congress, which is the naive rule this paper says fails. Hyphenated ranges are not expanded. So the network.csv vintage (2000-2022) and the 2021+ rebuild are different instruments with an unmeasured seam between them.
3. **The paper uses NAICS as an industry grouping.** The system has ruled NAICS to be linkage metadata only.

None of this is a validation of anything. The heuristics' accuracy is unreported, and the argmax always returns an answer.

bearings.paper_claim: LobbyView links lobbying to legislators only through bills: the bill numbers and titles found in report text are tied to bill sponsorship. No step observes a contact between a lobbyist and a member (Abstract; Section 2, steps 1-5).
bearings.system_side: The system already states that the member link is manufactured by joining each lobbied bill to its sponsor/cosponsor roster, so P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction and the link is REFUTED as evidence of influence. The module docstring defines the link as 'did this organization lobby a bill this member sponsored or cosponsored'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over fully. The paper's design is the upstream definition of the very table the system uses (network.csv, lob_id x bioguide x year x n_bills, 2000-2022). One discrepancy: the paper says 'sponsorship', but the system measured that the edges are sponsor plus all cosponsors (BECU 2021: 181 edges = 1 sponsor + 180 cosponsors of HR1996). So the paper's description understates how wide the join is.

bearings.paper_claim: Assigning a cited bill to the filing-year Congress fails: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is from the 112th Congress, not the 113th. LobbyView looks back over 3 prior Congresses and picks the candidate bill with the highest cosine similarity to the surrounding text (Eq. 1), then propagates the Congress across the report by majority vote.
bearings.system_side: In the 2021+ LDA rebuild, a formal citation goes to an earlier Congress only when an 'of 20XX' suffix follows it in the same segment. Every unsuffixed citation binds to the filing Congress, which is the rule the paper shows fails. There is no text-similarity lookback and no report-level propagation.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The risk is largest in first-session (odd-year) filings, where carryover bills from the prior Congress are most likely. The paper gives no rate for this error, so its size in Paul's finance rebuild is unknown (UNVERIFIED). The paper's argmax always returns a Congress, which conflicts with the system's never-guess, fail-closed style. Any extension should flag ambiguous citations rather than choose one.

bearings.paper_claim: Firms (clients) are grouped into industries by NAICS2 or SIC to compute per-industry, per-year Herfindahl indices (example run: NAICS, 1996-2011). Output is merged with Compustat and a trade-issue indicator.
bearings.system_side: The system classifies clients by name rules first. NAICS is used only as a fallback and flagged LOW confidence, because the LobbyView codebook gives NAICS no provenance; the standing finding is that it is entity-linkage metadata, not an industry classifier. A NAICS code that conflicts with the name is recorded as '+naics-conflict'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper treats NAICS industry assignment as usable for research aggregates, but it never validates the codes. That does not weaken the system's ruling for finance-client sides (bank vs CU), where one wrong label changes the adversary sets. Herfindahl outputs are industry-level descriptors and must not become edge weights (D-021).

bearings.paper_claim: LobbyView expands close bill numbers into ranges: the default takes numbers with the same prefix that differ by 10 or less, so the Mattel 2002 citation H.R.4182-4186 becomes 5 bills. It also matches titles and propagates the Congress across a report. No error rates are reported.
bearings.system_side: The rebuild's continuation parser accepts only comma, semicolon, ampersand and 'and' separators, so hyphenated ranges are not expanded. Congress binding works differently too (see above). The bridge looks used the LobbyView network.csv vintage (Kim pipeline) for 2021-2022 and the system's own rebuild for later windows.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This matters for any successor bridge prereg, which the brain says may only run on a new LobbyView vintage that extends past 2022. Such a prereg would be comparing dyad counts built by two different bill-resolution rule sets. The seam should be measured on an overlap year (2021) before any cross-vintage comparison. I found no recorded reconciliation in the notes I read (UNVERIFIED).

bearings.paper_claim: The Congress assignment takes an argmax over candidate Congresses and falls back to guessing the filing-year Congress when no bill matches. The author says this guess can be wrong, the title and range matching are heuristic, and the full methods description is deferred ('This document currently contains only some technical details of the database').
bearings.system_side: The contact-inference design requires a caveat that LDA does not disclose contacts and that scores are inferences. It bars treating LobbyView as validation. Paul's memos treat the LobbyView lineage as a cautionary chain, because an argmax always returns an answer.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Direct: this paper is the primary source for the lineage the memos cite. It supports using LobbyView only for definitions and identities (lob_id), never as ground truth for which members were contacted.

gaps_exposed: The 2021+ LDA rebuild has no prior-Congress lookback for unsuffixed bill citations. They bind to the filing Congress, which is the failure case the paper documents (H.R. 2577, 112th Congress, cited in a 2013 report). The system has never measured how often this happens in the finance rebuild.
Hyphenated bill ranges (e.g., H.R.4182-4186) are not expanded or counted as a diagnostic, so it is unknown how many lobbied bills the rebuild drops compared with the LobbyView vintage.

No overlap-year (2021) reconciliation between LobbyView network.csv dyads and the system's strict rebuild was found in the notes I read. A future bridge successor would cross an unmeasured instrument seam (UNVERIFIED).
The paper reports no error rates for any linkage heuristic. Both instruments, LobbyView and the rebuild, lack a hand-labelled precision/recall sample for bill-to-Congress resolution.
flags: The paper describes the link as bill 'sponsorship', but the system measured that LobbyView network edges are the sponsor plus all cosponsors. Any wording that inherits the paper's description understates the join and should say 'sponsored or cosponsored'.

D-021: the paper's design turns lobbying reports into member-linked edges and industry Herfindahl weights. Adopting either as an edge or weight source in the Melange graphs would conflict with D-021, which allows LDA as an identity source only (lob_id, client names).
Nothing in the paper licenses influence or contact language about lobbied members. The link is a bill-roster join, so P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction.
The 52,418 TRADE-issue report count has no window or year restriction in the text. It must not be quoted without stating that it covers 'all loaded reports, period unstated'.

The paper's argmax-plus-fallback Congress assignment always returns an answer. Copying it as-is would break the system's never-guess, fail-closed resolution style. Any adoption should flag ambiguous citations instead.
rel.paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's annotation, which cites it only in the contact-inference memos as a cautionary chain where an argmax always returns an answer. The paper itself says it assigns a Congress by argmax, guesses the filing year as a fallback, and reports no error rates. His broader position that LobbyView is the 'fundamental data source' for lobbying classification is stale against the system now, for three reasons. First, the system found that LobbyView NAICS is linkage metadata, not an industry classifier. Second, network linkage collapses after 2021 (2022 = 2,101 rows). Third, the member link is circular by construction. One more thing is not recorded in any note: Paul's own rebuild uses the naive filing-year Congress rule for unsuffixed citations, which is exactly what this paper warns against.

related.why: Kim & Kunisky's lobbying-network communities are built on the LobbyView bill-linkage this paper documents. Their member edges inherit the same sponsor/cosponsor join and Congress-assignment heuristics.
The positions dataset is keyed by the LobbyView lob_id and bill ids produced by this pipeline (111th-117th Congresses). Bill-to-Congress errors here pass straight into its position labels.
The LobbyView team's network evolution analysis (1999-2023) uses the same report and bill-linkage database and the same lobbyist disambiguation lineage.
It uses firm-level LobbyView data merged with Compustat, which is the merge this paper's herfindadd.py step describes.
It links LobbyView firm-level lobbying with FEC donations, the same pairing as the system's FEC-LDA bridge.
It is another pipeline for mining LDA records. Paul treats it as an introductory pipeline guide next to LobbyView.
